title: The Advocate's Defense and the Blind Man's Witness
english: Regarding the testimony to be given to a matter: Do you know the premise? Was it present? From where do you know the matter? And the very form teaches him to deny it.

So do they: How did you see? Who opened your eyes? But he, caring less for the threat, possessed more of the truth, and says: A certain man, called Jesus, having made clay, anointed my eyes and said to me: 'Go, wash in the Siloam' (John 9:6). And having gone, I washed, and I saw. He did not know the truth, but he recognized the benefit; he did not yet know the merit of the benefactor. A certain man, having made clay, anointed my eyes, and I see.

The Jews did not believe that he was blind and had seen, until his parents of the one who had seen were called. The diversion of malice into doubt brought away the truth. They call the parents of the blind man; malice by itself brings witnesses together. The parents of the blind man were called.

Again the same form of questioning: 'This is your son, whom you say was born blind? (John 9:25) How then does he see now?' They, having perceived the way of malice, that they are bringing threats, say to them: 'We know that this is our son; and that he was born blind we know; but how he sees now, or who opened his eyes, we do not know; he has age, ask him; he himself will speak about himself. And see the wisdom of God.'

So that they might not divert his voice, the one who had seen, as if he were a child, or as if he did not know how to speak, as in common courts, God caused him first to be shown in the age of law. 'He has age,' they say; 'ask him'; because immature advocates are needed, but those bringing maturity, they themselves become their own advocates.

His parents answered and said: 'This is our son, and that he was born blind we know.' The parents testified so that there would be no doubt that he was not blind. 'He has age, ask him; he himself will speak about himself.' They call him again, he says, a second time, and say to him: 'What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?' He, moreover, having clothed himself with the zeal of God, unfolds the question, and as if for those unworthy of an answer, not worthy of a word, but what does he say to them? 'I have already said to you, and...'

“You did not hear; why do you wish to hear me again? Do you not also wish to become his disciples?” (John 7:40). And he who has not yet heard Christ's teaching imitates it. For the Jews, having surrounded the Savior in Solomon's Colonnade during the festivals (John 10:23), said to him: “How long will you lift up our soul? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.” He says to them: “I said to you, and you did not hear; why do you wish to hear again?” And see the piety of the advocate.

Because he paid attention to the malice of the Jews, for they do everything and shape threats and fear to be cast upon him so that he might not confess himself teacher, he says to them: “I said to you already, and you did not hear; why do you wish to hear again? Do you not also wish to become his disciples?” By saying, “Do you not also?”, he showed that the “I am” is being confessed. Let every Christian coming from Hellenism have this voice. For when a Greek meets you, having an ancient habit of error, and says to you, “Become a Christian,” say to him, “Yes; do you not also wish to become?”

The goal, therefore, of the one who recovered both soul and body, was such: “I said to you already, and you did not hear; why do you wish to hear me again? Do you not also wish to become his disciples?” Instead of [saying], “Stay this far from turning to me,” for I also more eagerly expect you, having been changed, to confess Christ himself according to the truth.

Then what [was] against him from the Jews? They mocked him and said: “You are a disciple of that man, but we are disciples of Moses. We know that God spoke to Moses; but this one we do not know from where he is.” Consider the multitude of the objectors, and the power of one standing against them. And the advocate of the truth did not be silent again, but stood firm, saying, “For in this it is wonderful,” saying, that you do not know from where he is, and he opened my eyes (John 9:35). If this man were not from God, he would not have been able to do anything. He stands struggling, and God is the overseer and the judge; many are terrible against one strong man, an unbelieving cloud against a single drop of faith. From the age, he says, it was not heard that someone opened the eyes of one born blind (John 9:32). If this man were not from God, he would not have been able to do anything. Because you magnify yourselves, he says, in the teaching of Moses. He does not mention Moses at all, so that—
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: From Human Supporter to Divine Witness
english: Let him not be provoked. For he says, 'From the beginning of the age it has not been heard that anyone opened the eyes of one born blind' (John 9:32), that is, 'Who else opened [them], a prophet?' Nor did they see the superiority, nor the comparison. But as much as this man held to the truth, so much did they not cease from shamelessness.

Since they were not able to deny it, they endeavored instead to cover it, and they say: 'Give glory to God; we know that this man is a sinful human.' The glory of the Son is the glory of the Father, and the glory is undivided. He is contending, having the good struggle toward the Jews. They say to him, 'Give glory to God.' How? By our law? And is it right to benefit another and for another to be glorified? 'Give glory to God.' Another benefactor, and to another should I give glory? They confessed that Jesus made clay and anointed his eyes; does the one who opened [them] confess, and should I give the glory to another? Why should I give glory to God? Because this work is the work of God. Therefore, seeing, you confess that Christ is God. 'Give glory to God.' For if the work is of God, and to Him the glory is owed, the maker of the work is God Himself. 'Give glory to God.' We know that this man is a sinful human.

The once-blind man answered them: 'If he is a sinner, I do not know; one thing I know, that being blind, now I see' (John 9:25). He spoke with such boldness that they ordered him to be cast out. And they cast him out, says the evangelist, out (John 9:34). Blessed is the one set apart from the synagogue of evildoers. And see what happens. Because he contended the good struggle, and sympathized with the glory of God, and confessed the Savior gloriously with much boldness; and while his theater was being filled with wrestling matches, the wrestler was cast out without receiving the crown, and the referee meets him outside.

For Jesus heard, he says, that they had cast him out; and finding him, he says to him. Oh, the speech of the one finding him! That which error destroys, truth finds. Why then did he meet him? The Savior saw a soul full of gratitude; he saw a soul not yet having been made known to speak concerning God, but considering [him] to be some faithful prophet; for he asks concerning the Christ. And what does he say about him? That he is a prophet. And the Savior said this: 'If [you] consider him a prophet, and anth...'

Suspecting a human, he struggles thus: what will he do if he learns the glory of the deity? If, suspecting a human and calling him a prophet, he has brought so much support for the sake of truth, and has undergone such a great struggle without having yet been instructed, but having been enlightened by grace alone: understand him, that if, thinking to support a human, he did not depart from the truth, he will speak evangelically: 'In the beginning was the Word; and the Word was with God, and the God was the Word' (John 1:1); what will result? Therefore, moreover, the Lord corrected him toward knowledge, having received the struggle, and having sealed the faith for him.

The Savior answers him; for this one did not recognize the character. For when He sent him to the pool of Siloam to wash, He sent him blind; but when he returned seeing, he did not see the Savior because of the crowd being mixed there, but immediately, before seeing the Master, having been called into the struggle, he struggled. But the Master made clay before washing him himself, and anointed his eyes, so that he might complete what was lacking. When therefore He sent him out, Christ finding him, said to him: 'Do you believe in the Son of God?' (John 9:35). For it is not necessary for you to believe in a struggling man as a prophet, but as the Son of God.

That one, not having recognized the face, recognized the voice. 'Do you believe,' He says, 'in the Son of God?' He knew the voice, and with delight he cried out, 'And who is He, Lord, so that I may believe in Him?' Why do you believe Him saying to the believer: 'Do you believe in the Son of God?' 'I know that your word is true; yet even if you should tell me the knowledge, I do not waver in believing you.' 'And who is He, Lord, so that I may believe in Him?' And the prophet replied: 'And you have seen Him, and the one speaking with you, He is that one.'

He who supported from within, discourses from without: 'Do you believe in the Son of God?' But the one enlightened in both body and mind said: 'And who is He, Lord, so that I may believe in Him?' And the one answering said to him: 'And you have seen Him, and the one speaking with you, He is that one.' And he said: 'I believe, Lord,' and he worshiped Him. These things are said to me so that you all may learn to follow a good teacher, and to imitate a good shepherd, and to struggle for the sake of truth; for your [one]...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Thief's Confession and the Lesson of Piety
english: The struggle happens in cooperation with the Great Shepherd. You marveled that a blind man became a co-witness of the truth having been benefited; you marveled at the robber who, before the benefit, co-witnessed with Christ. For always a divine soul, zealously seeking the truth, opens many mouths co-witnessing to the truth by its own reliability.

Christ was hanging on the cross, and two robbers, one on the right and one of good repute, and the Jews are slandering, the chief priests are blaspheming: 'Behold the King of the Jews' (Matt 27:42); and again, 'If he is the King of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe in him' (Matt 27:42); and again, 'He saved others, but he cannot save himself' (Mark 15:31). Likewise, the one crucified robber also blasphemed, saying: 'If you are the Son of God, save yourself and us' (Luke 23:39). But the other robber said nothing, punishing the condemned by his silence.

Since therefore the chief priests and the scribes, knowing the law, but rather being ignorant, those who ought to have confessed Christ from the prophetic readings, did not confess; God opens an unexpected mouth upon the cross, co-witnessing to the truth. And see what he does. He does not even first hear the voice of Christ, and this one co-witnesses, and then he is crowned. For two robbers were crucified, he says, one on the right and one of good repute; and the Savior was in the middle like a yoke of truth, crowning indeed the one confessing, but condemning the one blaspheming.

And behold the wonderful thing. Of the scribes and the chief priests blaspheming Christ, and saying: 'If he is the King of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe in him' (Matt 27:42); and of the other robber: 'If you are the Son of God, save yourself and us' (Luke 23:39); the one of good repute says nothing. For the two robbers were icons of the people of the Jews and of ours. For the one blasphemes and is condemned; but the one believes and repents and is saved. Therefore the one of good repute, the brother of the Jewish robbery, says [nothing] (for the ignorant Jews were a robber people, as the Savior testifies saying: 'My house shall be called a house of prayer; but you have made it a robbers' den' [Matt 21:13]); and the choice of the first is Jewish; but the choice of the second is Christian.

Driven by evil, but seizing salvation through repentance; thus speaks the ignorant thief, having a Jewish choice: 'If you are the Son of God, save yourself and us, by coming down from the cross.' But the other, the discerning one, is found—the one responsible in the courtroom, a judge at the cross; but also teaching the fear of God.

For the first cry of the thief to the fellow-robber says: 'Do you not even fear God, since you are in the same judgment?' And 'We indeed [are judged] justly, for we receive what is worthy of what we have done'; but this one did nothing strange. What are you saying? You, stealing outside, condemn here? You, murdering outside, teach fear here? 'Do you not even fear God?' Learn the cross of Christ, so that the voice may become to you a teacher of piety.

For see the wonderful thing: the thief says to the fellow-robber: 'Do you not even fear God?' He proclaims God himself crucified with them, and suffering long-sufferingly for the sake of humanity. And that regarding the Savior he says: 'Do you not even fear God?' Learn from the following: 'Do you not even fear God, since you are in the same judgment?' And 'We indeed [are judged] justly, for we receive what is worthy of what we have done'; but this one did nothing strange.

I say these things so that you may learn to toil for the sake of piety, and to show zeal both in the house and in the marketplace, and to contend for Christ, so that you also may receive from him the crown of righteousness, like this discerning thief. For listen to him toward the blasphemous fellow-robber: 'Do you not even fear God, since you are in the same judgment?' And 'We indeed [are judged] justly, for we receive what is worthy of what we have done'; but this one did nothing strange.

And he said to Jesus, 'Remember me, Lord, when you come in your kingdom' (Luke 23:42). Did you see a true sympathy? Did you see how he, the Christ, confessed God truly? 'Remember me, Lord, when you come in your kingdom.' He confesses his own evils and sympathizes with the Lord.

You were tortured so much, thief, before the ruler, so that you might confess the robberies, and the murders, and the thefts which you did, even if you did not confess; and here you say, without tortures, 'We indeed [are judged] justly, for we receive what is worthy of what we have done'? Through ten thousand tortures you only just confessed before the ruler; and here, having no one to compel you, easily...
